_comment.intent: P0 #2 - TikTok initialisation is rejected for every host app and the error is discarded. Confirm-first: the digits-only validator claim comes from one audit source and has not been reproduced.

summary: TikTok: confirm and fix the silent initialisation failure
description:
The TikTok module passes the host app's bundle identifier as TikTok's app id. The pinned TikTok Business SDK appears to accept only digits in that field, so a bundle id like com.company.app reduces to nothing and initialisation is rejected. The TikTok SDK reports that failure through a completion callback which the module ignores, so nothing is logged and nothing fails: the module reports as configured and sends no events for the rest of the session.

If that is right, TikTok attribution has never worked through this module, for any host app. It has not been reproduced yet, so confirming it is the first piece of work here and the rest only follows if it is confirmed.

Acceptance criteria:
- The behaviour of the pinned TikTok SDK when given a bundle identifier as app id is confirmed or refuted
- If confirmed: the identifiers TikTok actually requires are supplied by the host app through the SDK's existing configuration entry point, and are documented
- A rejected or failed TikTok initialisation is surfaced rather than discarded
- A test fails when TikTok initialisation is rejected - checking that the module loads is not enough
- TikTok events are confirmed arriving from a real app after integration
- If the reading turns out to be wrong, the ticket closes with the evidence recorded and no code change

_comment.intent: P0 #3 - ATT gate records a prompt that was never shown as answered, waits unbounded, and is not idempotent despite being documented as such. Most corroborated finding in the audit set.

summary: ATT: stop recording an unanswered prompt as answered, and make requestATT() safe to call twice
description:
Three problems sit in the App Tracking Transparency step, and each one costs attribution for the whole life of an install.

The prompt can only be shown while the app is in the foreground. If it is requested at any other moment, iOS returns "not determined" - meaning the user was never asked. The SDK stores that as the final answer, so that install never sees the prompt again, on any later launch. It has no advertising identifier from then on: AppsFlyer, Meta and TikTok all lose it, and TikTok tracking stays switched off permanently. There is no recovery short of the user deleting and reinstalling the app.

There is a retry path that waits for the app to become active, and that wait has no limit. If the app never becomes active, the call never returns and AppsFlyer never starts - no install event, no attribution for that session.

requestATT() is documented as safe to call more than once and it is not: a second call re-runs the entire AppsFlyer startup. A host app that ties it to the app becoming active - a reasonable reading of the current guide - re-runs it on every single foreground.

No test covers any of this today; nothing in the suite calls requestATT() at all.

Acceptance criteria:
- An unanswered ATT prompt is never stored as the outcome; that install is asked again on a later launch
- Only a real user answer - allowed, denied or restricted - is treated as final
- The wait for the app to become active cannot leave the call hanging indefinitely, and the behaviour when it gives up is decided and documented
- Calling requestATT() more than once does not restart AppsFlyer, and the documented behaviour matches what the code does
- All three paths are covered by tests that fail if the behaviour regresses
- An app that shows the prompt late, or in the background, ends up in a recoverable state rather than a permanent one

_comment.intent: P0 #4 - AppsFlyer never starts silently when identity cannot be resolved, plus the banned Purchases.shared read and the empty-rcId path that still runs vendor hooks.
_comment.sequencing: Should land after the identity-contract tests story, so the change is made against tests that can catch a mistake.

summary: AppsFlyer: never fail to start silently, and remove the banned identity fallback
description:
AppsFlyer startup depends on the RevenueCat user id. If that id cannot be read, the startup step gives up: no log, no retry, AppsFlyer never starts. The app looks completely healthy and produces no install event and no attribution.

Two identity problems sit in the same path and make it worse.

When the id cannot be read, the identity cache falls back to reading RevenueCat's current user id directly. That is the read this package explicitly forbids, and it is not the same value: it returns the aliased id rather than the original one. Two different ids can therefore reach AppsFlyer as the customer user id, and which one sticks depends on which write lands last - the join key between AppsFlyer, RevenueCat and Amplitude decided by a race.

When configuration cannot resolve the id at all, it substitutes an empty string and carries on running the Meta and TikTok setup anyway. Those vendors are then configured with no user identity for that session, and nothing reports it.

The desired outcome is that identity failure is loud, bounded and consistent. Silently half-succeeding is not an acceptable state for the step that owns attribution.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every path where AppsFlyer does not start is logged with the reason it did not start
- A failure to resolve the user id is notified to the developers via logs or exception
- The user id reaching AppsFlyer comes from one source only, and no path can produce two different values for it
- Configuring with a missing user id has a decided, documented behaviour - fail, skip the vendors, or proceed - instead of being an accident
- Tests cover the failed-lookup and empty-id paths
- Someone reading the logs of a host app can tell whether attribution started, without checking the AppsFlyer dashboard

_comment.intent: P0 #5 - the async setup window: release crash on early events, no readiness signal, and a check-then-act guard that lets two concurrent configures through.
_comment.decisions: Filippo 2026-07-28: early events are queued and flushed in tracking order; on setup failure they are discarded and the failure is surfaced via log or raised error. Queue bound left as a documentation requirement.
_comment.kickoff_note: An unhandled error raised from a tracking call in release is the crash this story removes - 'raised error' must mean something the host can catch or observe, not a fatal one.

summary: Bootstrap: one configuration, a readiness signal, and no crash for early events
description:
Setting the SDK up is asynchronous and waits on a network round trip. Three problems live inside that window.

An event tracked before setup completes crashes the app. Not an assertion that disappears in a release build - it crashes in production too. The integration guide tells host apps to track a splash-screen event at exactly that moment.

Nothing tells a host when setup is done, so every integrating app invents its own coordination - in practice by wrapping the call in a background task, which is the shape the current API forces. Two of those wrappers both get past the "already configured?" check, because that check happens before the first suspension point. The result is RevenueCat configured twice, two analytics clients, vendor setup run twice, and a subscription listener that is never cancelled and duplicates every subscription update for the life of the process.

There is no supported answer to "the app wants to send an event and the SDK isn't ready yet". There is one now: those events are held and sent once setup finishes, in the order the app tracked them. An app should never have to know whether the SDK is ready before it can record something, and nothing tracked during startup should be lost or reordered. If setup fails the held events are not sent - but that has to reach whoever integrated the SDK, rather than the events quietly disappearing.

Acceptance criteria:
- Tracking an event before setup completes never crashes the app, in any build configuration
- Events tracked before the SDK is ready are held, and sent once setup completes, in the order they were tracked; any limit on how many are held is documented
- This holds for every way an event can be sent, including the generated tracking methods
- When setup fails, held events are discarded rather than sent, and the developer is told through a log or a raised error instead of the events disappearing silently
- Two concurrent setup calls produce exactly one configuration: one RevenueCat, one analytics client, one run of the vendor setup, one subscription listener
- A host app can ask whether the SDK is ready or wait until it is, and can tell a failed setup from one still in progress
- Tests cover concurrent setup, events tracked during setup, and the order they arrive in

_comment.intent: P0 #6 - the test guarding the identity ordering contract cannot fail, plus two more test doubles that record nothing. Should land before the AppsFlyer story changes that path.

summary: Make the tests that guard the identity contract able to fail
description:
The rule this package exists to protect is an ordering rule: AppsFlyer must be told the customer user id before AppsFlyer is started. Reversing those two steps is what shipped thousands of installs a day with no customer user id and broke the joins between AppsFlyer, RevenueCat and Amplitude.

The test that claims to guard that rule cannot fail. It checks the final state only, and the test double it checks against records no ordering - so swapping the two lines in the real code leaves the suite green. The one guarantee the suite is supposed to give is the one it does not give.

Two more of the same kind sit next to it. The analytics test double never records the user id it is handed, because its setter assigns the value to itself; as a result the main path of the cross-attribution step has never actually executed in a test, in either direction. And the test named after the pre-configuration crash asserts something unrelated to it.

Acceptance criteria:
- The order in which AppsFlyer receives the customer user id and the start call is asserted, not just the end state
- Reversing those two calls in the source makes the suite fail - demonstrated on this ticket, not assumed
- The analytics test double records what it was given, and both branches of the cross-attribution step are covered
- The placeholder test either tests what its name says or is removed
- Every test added or fixed here is shown to fail against deliberately broken code before it is accepted
- Any other test double standing in for a vendor is checked for the same defect

_comment.intent: P0 #7 - the canonical integration guide does not work; roughly nine of twenty-four samples do not compile. Major rather than Critical: nothing is broken in production, but it blocks adoption.
_comment.companion: The last AC is what backlog ticket 8 (ExampleApp target in CI, P1) actually delivers - link them when that is created.

summary: Integration guide: make the documented path actually work
description:
An engineer following the canonical integration guide cannot get past step 2. The configuration object in the guide names three members that do not exist and leaves out required ones - two of which, the AppsFlyer app id and the OneLink id, are not documented anywhere in the repository at all, so there is no way to discover them except by reading the package source.

It does not improve further down: a Firebase setup hook that does not exist, a TikTok hook with a signature that does not exist, a property used as if it were optional and synchronous when it is neither, an await in a place where the language does not allow one, URL forwarding wired to the wrong SDK, and prerequisites naming the wrong iOS and Xcode versions. Roughly nine of the guide's twenty-four code samples do not compile.

Around it, the README teaches the exact RevenueCat access pattern the package forbids, a second older guide documents methods that do not exist, and the contributor instructions tell people to validate their work with a command that cannot succeed on a Mac.

The cost is paid once per integration, by a different team each time, and every one of those teams ends up asking the SDK author. Getting this SDK into every app in the portfolio is the stated goal for the year, and this document is the first thing each of those teams reads.

Acceptance criteria:
- An engineer can integrate the SDK from the guide alone, without reading the package source
- Every code sample in the guide compiles, checked mechanically rather than by eye
- Every required configuration value is documented, including the AppsFlyer ones missing today
- One integration guide exists, not two
- The README and the contributor instructions no longer contradict the package's own rules
- The changelog records the breaking changes in 2.0.0 that it currently omits
- A sample that goes stale is caught before release rather than by the next integrating team
